guides.title: Orchestration topology trade-offs
guides.summary: Loops, graphs, supervisors and parallel workers solve different coordination problems; topology should be chosen from dependency structure rather than architectural fashion.
guides.mentalModel: An orchestration topology is a control-flow decision. Use the simplest structure that represents task dependencies, state ownership, retry boundaries and verification without paying unnecessary coordination overhead.
guides.whyItMatters: Multi-agent diagrams can look sophisticated while hiding basic responsibility problems. A linear loop is easier to observe and recover than a graph, while a graph becomes valuable when work has real branches, joins, independent stages or conditional recovery. Supervisors add centralized coordination but can become bottlenecks; peer-to-peer delegation distributes control but makes global state and accountability harder.

sections.title: Match topology to dependencies and failure boundaries
sections.body: Start by drawing the task dependencies without agent labels. If one state transition naturally follows another, a loop or sequence is usually sufficient. Introduce branches for conditional paths, parallel nodes for independent work and joins only when outputs have a clear reconciliation contract. Define who owns shared state, where retries occur and which node verifies completion before choosing the coordination mechanism.

sections.title: Example: research pipeline versus open-ended incident response
sections.body: A research workflow with collect, extract, synthesize and verify stages may fit a simple graph with one parallel evidence-gathering branch and a clear join. An incident-response assistant with changing observations may be better modeled as one bounded loop that repeatedly diagnoses and acts. Splitting it into many agents would add handoffs without creating real independence.

failureModes: Choosing a multi-agent graph before identifying actual task dependencies.
Adding supervisor layers that repeat work already visible in shared state.
Creating parallel branches with no deterministic merge or conflict policy.
heuristics: Draw data and state dependencies before assigning agents.
Prefer a loop until branching or independent concurrency has measurable value.
Define join, retry and ownership semantics before adding parallel nodes.
takeaways: Topology is a consequence of workflow structure.
More nodes create more coordination and observability cost.
Simple control flow is a baseline that complex orchestration must beat.

guides.title: Multimodal iteration
guides.summary: Text, image, audio and other modalities need iterative review against cross-modal meaning and production constraints, not independent generation followed by assembly.
guides.mentalModel: A multimodal artifact is one communication system. Each modality has its own generation constraints, but quality depends on whether the pieces agree on meaning, hierarchy, timing and audience experience.
guides.whyItMatters: A good script paired with a misleading image is still a bad lesson. Generated captions can contradict visuals, diagrams can introduce labels the text never explains, and aesthetically strong media can overwhelm the instructional point. Multimodal work therefore needs a shared brief and review loop that checks relationships between modalities rather than approving each asset in isolation.

sections.title: Iterate from a shared communication contract
sections.body: Define the learning or product objective, key claims, audience and hierarchy before generating individual assets. Produce a first pass across modalities, then review alignment: does the image support the claim, does narration match visible state, is critical information duplicated or missing, and can the artifact still work with accessibility alternatives? Revise the weakest relationship rather than regenerating everything at once.

sections.title: Example: an animated explanation of a context window
sections.body: The narration says old messages are being compacted, but the animation merely fades random tokens. A cross-modal review catches that the visual implies deletion rather than state-preserving compression. The animation is revised to show selected constraints and evidence surviving into a smaller representation while the script remains unchanged.

failureModes: Reviewing text, image and audio quality independently without checking semantic alignment.
Using decorative media that competes with the information hierarchy.
Regenerating all modalities after one mismatch and losing already-correct work.
heuristics: Give every modality the same objective, claims and audience constraints.
Review cross-modal contradictions explicitly before polishing style.
Change the smallest failing relationship during iteration.
takeaways: Multimodal quality is relational, not the sum of separate asset scores.
Shared briefs preserve meaning across media.
Iteration should target mismatches between modalities as well as local defects.

guides.title: Open and closed model trade-offs
guides.summary: Open-weight and hosted closed models offer different control, operational burden, data boundaries and capability economics; the right choice depends on the system constraint.
guides.mentalModel: Model access is an architecture choice across control and responsibility. Greater deployment control can improve customization and data locality while transferring serving, security and update obligations to your team.
guides.whyItMatters: Teams often reduce the decision to price or benchmark quality. In practice, hosted models may provide strong capability, rapid updates and managed scaling but impose provider constraints and external data boundaries. Open-weight models can be inspected, adapted and self-hosted, but require infrastructure, evaluation and patching discipline. Hybrid systems may use both when workloads have different privacy, latency or capability needs.

sections.title: Compare the full operating model
sections.body: Evaluate candidate approaches across workload quality, latency, total serving cost, context and tool features, deployment location, data-handling requirements, update control, observability, fine-tuning needs and operational expertise. Include the cost of evaluation and migration when providers or model versions change. The choice should be revisited when constraints change rather than treated as an ideological commitment.

sections.title: Example: private document extraction plus complex reasoning
sections.body: A company keeps sensitive document parsing on a self-hosted smaller model inside its environment, then sends only approved structured facts to a hosted stronger model for non-sensitive synthesis. The split adds complexity, but it is justified by a concrete data boundary and capability requirement rather than a blanket preference for one model category.

failureModes: Comparing API price with raw compute cost while ignoring operations and utilization.
Assuming self-hosting automatically solves privacy without access and logging controls.
Choosing a provider category once and never re-evaluating workload fit.
heuristics: Compare total operating responsibility, not only model quality and unit price.
Tie deployment choice to explicit data, latency and control requirements.
Keep evaluation portable enough to compare alternatives when the stack changes.
takeaways: Open versus closed is a system trade-off, not a universal ranking.
More deployment control also means more operational responsibility.
Hybrid architectures can be justified when different workload slices have different constraints.

guides.title: Memory expiry and invalidation
guides.summary: Durable memory should stop influencing decisions when its evidence becomes stale, its scope ends or stronger information supersedes it.
guides.mentalModel: Every memory has a validity condition. Expiry can be time-based, event-based or authority-based, and invalidation is as important as writing because stale memory can be more dangerous than no memory.
guides.whyItMatters: Persistent assistants can confidently reuse facts that were once correct: a project role changes, a policy expires, a customer preference is reversed or a workflow checkpoint is completed. Without expiry and supersession, old state remains semantically relevant enough to be retrieved and can silently contradict authoritative current data.

sections.title: Attach validity and invalidation triggers to memory classes
sections.body: For each durable memory type, define what ends its validity: a time horizon, a source update, completion of a workflow, explicit user change or stronger authoritative record. Store update time and provenance, mark superseded records so retrieval excludes them from current state, and periodically test whether high-impact memory classes still resolve to authoritative evidence.

sections.title: Example: temporary project access remembered forever
sections.body: An assistant stores that a contractor may access a private project during a six-week engagement. If that permission is remembered without expiry, later tasks may incorrectly expose project information. The durable record instead carries an engagement end condition and is invalidated automatically when the access system reports the contractor is no longer active.

failureModes: Giving all memories infinite lifetime because deletion feels risky.
Deleting historical records without separating audit history from effective current state.
Using only fixed time-to-live when a source update should invalidate memory immediately.
heuristics: Define expiry and supersession when defining each memory schema.
Retrieve only effective current memory while keeping audit history separate when needed.
Prefer authoritative event-driven invalidation for high-impact state.
takeaways: Stale remembered state can be more harmful than missing context.
Expiry, supersession and audit retention are different responsibilities.

guides.title: Customer support copilot
guides.summary: A support copilot should increase operator leverage by retrieving evidence, structuring cases and drafting actions while keeping source authority and consequential decisions explicit.
guides.mentalModel: A copilot is decision support before full automation. It assembles verified context and proposes bounded next steps, while the human or runtime policy still owns approvals, exceptions and high-impact actions.
guides.whyItMatters: Customer support is attractive for AI because work is repetitive and knowledge-heavy, but real tickets contain exceptions, account state and policy consequences. Jumping directly to autonomous resolution hides whether the system actually retrieves the right policy, identifies uncertainty and escalates correctly. A copilot stage creates operational value while producing the evidence needed to decide which parts can later be automated safely.

sections.title: Build leverage around the support decision
sections.body: Start with classification, account-context retrieval, knowledge search, case summarization and response drafting. Show controlling sources and uncertainty to the operator, and keep state-changing tools behind explicit policy. Measure acceptance, edits, retrieval failures, escalation reasons and resolution outcomes. Only move stable low-risk actions across the automation boundary after postconditions and exception rates are well understood.

sections.title: Example: refund request with a policy exception
sections.body: The copilot identifies the customer's plan, retrieves the current refund policy and drafts a response, but notices the purchase was made during a special migration period with conflicting guidance. It surfaces both sources and recommends escalation instead of inventing a definitive answer or issuing money automatically.

failureModes: Hiding source evidence and asking agents to trust a generated support summary.
Automating refunds before understanding exception and reconciliation paths.
Measuring draft speed while ignoring operator edits and wrong-source retrieval.
heuristics: Expose controlling evidence next to proposed support actions.
Use copilot telemetry to identify which decisions are stable enough for automation.
Keep consequential actions behind explicit tool, policy and escalation boundaries.
takeaways: Copilot is a useful intermediate operating model, not a failure to automate.
Support quality depends on current knowledge and account state.
Measured human-assisted workflows reveal where safe automation boundaries actually are.
